title: MB5-06127
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX, who is a 50-year-old citizen of Serbia, is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: Ms. XXXX XXXX, who is a 50-year-old citizen of Serbia, is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting her claim for refugee protection. The Appellant has not requested to present new evidence and has not requested an oral hearing.

Given the allegations of Ms. XXXX, before rendering a decision in this appeal, the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) carefully reviewed the IRB Chairperson's Guidelines on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution1.

With respect to the RPD's determination on country conditions applied to the Appellant's allegations and particular circumstances, for a number of reasons the RPD concluded that the Appellant would faces less than a serious risk of persecution if she were to return to Serbia, seek state protection and live apart from her husband. I am in agreement with this assessment, therefore, pursuant to ss. 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD, namely, that Ms. XXXX XXXX is neither a "Convention Refugee" pursuant to s. 96 of IRPA nor a "person in need of protection" pursuant to s. 97 of the IRPA.

The Appellant, who was born, raised and lived in XXXX XXXX, Serbia, alleges that she is at risk of being attacked and potentially killed by her husband, identified as Mr. XXXX XXXX, because the Appellant has left this relationship and MrXXXX XXXX allegedly seeks her return and has allegedly threatened her over the phone.

The Appellant alleges that after marrying Mr. XXXX the violence and controlling aspects of the relationship were regular occurrences. The Appellant and Mr. XXXX had a son, identified as XXXX, who was born in 1998 and who has also suffered at the hands of Mr. XXXX.

The Appellant arrived in Canada in XXXX 2013 on a visitor's visa and applied for Canada's protection in November 2013. The RPD first heard and denied this claim in February 2014 (RPD Record, p. 120-129). In the area of the domestic abuse determination, which was the first of three protection issues addressed, the RPD determined based on testimony that Mr. XXXX was not interested in pursuing the Appellant and specifically that the evidence showed that Mr. XXXX "is not seeking to stop her from leaving him and would not seek to harm her in the future" (RPD Record, p. 123).

The Appellant appealed to the RAD (RPD Record, p. 132-141) focusing on the domestic abuse issue identifying new evidence of the actions of Mr. XXXX and arguing that the RPD erred in its conclusion that while Mr. XXXX may have stopped attacking the Appellant in the period prior to her departure and did not seek to stop her from leaving, this "is not at all sufficient basis upon which to conclude that the danger of persecution has largely disappeared" (RPD Record, p. 139).

The RAD concludes that prior abuse and unpredictable behaviour on Mr. XXXX part could establish the serious possibility of future persecution. The RAD notes, however, that some credibility issues remain and sets out that the issue of state protection requires a review prior to a final determination on this domestic abuse issue therefore the appeal was allowed and the case was returned to the RPD (RPD Record, p. 140).

The RPD heard the returned claim in September 2015 and denied the claim in an oral decision. This decision was appealed by submitting a Notice of Appeal, which was received by the RAD on November 3, 2015.

The Appellant in its appeal focuses on the issue of domestic violence and argues that the RPD's analysis includes errors related to its determination that the Appellant "could re-establish herself in Serbia without difficulty". The Appellant also argues that the Appellant erred in its state protection analysis.

In terms of an outcome from this appeal, the Appellant seeks to have the RAD 'set aside' the RPD decision and recognize the Appellant as requiring Canada's protection. Alternatively, the Appellant seeks to have the file returned to the RPD for a 'hearing and redetermination' by a different panel.

With respect to the role and function of the RAD, in a recent Federal Court of Appeal decision related to jurisprudence on this issue, the conclusion is that the RAD must apply the correctness standard in its review of RPD decisions. At the same time, in the area of a credibility assessment in which RPD had the advantage of an oral hearing, the RAD may show deference to the conclusion of the RPD.2 ANALYSIS Core Issue: Did the Board err in its determination that the Appellant would face less than a serious risk of persecution if she were to return to Serbia, seek state protection and live apart from her husband?
paragraphs.heading_before: ROLE AND FUNCTION OF THE RAD

paragraphs.text: The determinative issue identified by the RPD in this case is that it would be possible for the Appellant to return to XXXX XXXX, seek state protection and perhaps initially live in a shelter before securing employment towards re-establishing herself at a separate residence.

With respect to the specific circumstance of the Appellant, she is a 50 year old woman who alleges a risk at the hands of her 58 year old husband. Her son is now 18 years old (born in XXXX 1998) and no longer factors into this determination. In fact, the Appellant notes that her son is athletic (good at soccer) who has faced problems with his father as well and therefore perhaps in time he could become an aid to his mother in terms of security, moral and financial support. The thrust of the RPD decision is that the Appellant could find employment and live with the support of those around her including her brother in XXXX XXXX and with the aid of others including her family in Canada.

The Appellant's core argument is that the RPD analysis is "erroneous and absurd" (Appellant's Memorandum, paragraph 11) because state protection in Serbia is inadequate and there is a serious possibility that Mr. XXXX will seek to persecute the Appellant should she return. According to the Appellant, "...returning the Applicant to XXXX XXXX would simply return her to the man who has terrorized her life for the past twenty years" (Appellant's Memorandum, paragraph 14).

I conclude that Canada's international commitment to protect those fleeing persecution is surrogate protection. Canada's responsibility can be evoked after it is determined that the Appellant county of origin cannot provide adequate protection. To reach this determination, the individual circumstances of the Appellant must be assessed. In this case the key issue is the objective risk presented by Mr. XXXX (the agent of persecution's 'profile' - Appellant's Record, p. 30), the specific circumstances of the Appellant and the adequacy of the instruments of state protection in XXXX XXXX.

In this case the agent of persecution, Mr. XXXX is identified as a 58 year old man who is university educated, until recently employed as a high school teacher and who does not have a criminal record. It is noted that in this case domestic abuse and violence did not escalate in the past to the point where the police were ever called or the Appellant required "hospitalization" (RPD Record, p. 7). I note, however, that there appears to be an evolution in the risk. The thrust of the first RPD decision sets out that the Mr. XXXX was disinterested in the Appellant and was not opposed to the Appellant moving out of the shared residence. This was in a situation where the domestic violence was kept relatively hidden which can be seen in the situation where the Appellant's brother was thought unaware of the domestic violence (RPD Record, p. 123) and no threats against the Appellant were noted by the Appellant after the Appellant left Serbia but prior to the first RPD decision (RPD Record, p. 124).

With the appeal of the first RPD decision, evidence is cited which sets out that the Appellant's son is being regularly beaten and Mr. XXXX is now being abusive and demands that the Appellant 'return home' (Appellant's Record, p. 116-117). I note that with the latest RPD decision (September 2015) it is noted that Mr. XXXX has since threatened the Appellant in phone calls (RPD Record, p. 7). The task becomes, therefore, for the RPD to balance the potential actions of Mr. XXXX compared to instruments of state protection in XXXX XXXX a situation where the Appellant would not be living with Mr. XXXX.

One of the ways to reach a determination on the objective risk presented by Mr. XXXX is to review his past history. It is noted that Mr. XXXX was twice married in the past and was abusive each time. When there was a breakup, however, Mr. XXXX did not pursue or persecute these woman.

When questioned on this issue, the Appellant argues that this should not be taken as an indicator of the future behaviour of Mr. XXXX because, in one case, the ex-wife left the country. With respect to the second ex-wife, the Appellant argues that she remarried and the new husband "could logically deter" Mr. XXXX "as that woman's husband would have protected her" (Appellant's Memorandum, paragraph 21).

As I understand this argument, Mr. XXXX can be deterred from causing persecution by a husband if the Appellant were to remarry but in this case the Appellant would be returning to XXXX XXXX as a woman alone, although some level of support might be expected from her 'sick' brother, therefore she would be at risk, even in a woman's shelter.

I must conclude that the logic of the Appellant's argument in this case establishes a fundamentally low threshold of risk because the same deterrence is operative in both cases (ex-wife and Appellant). This is to say that the deterrence faced by Mr. XXXX is related to the intervention of the police. Unless the Appellant is arguing that Mr. XXXX fears vigilante justice on the part of the ex-wife's husband, ultimately an ex-wife in the same geographic area as the agent of persecution, which is to say in a city of approximately 100,000 in the municipal area (XXXX XXXX), is often vulnerable to attack as she goes about her daily activities. In the normal course of events the deterrence faced by the agent of persecution is not some active and vigilant defence of the wife by the husband, but being arrested, charged and punished by mechanisms of state security.

In this case of the second ex-wife, Mr. XXXX did not assault the ex-wife but the Appellant is arguing that now, in the case of the Appellant, there is a serious possibility that Mr. XXXX will attack the Appellant even though they have now lived apart for nearly three years (since the Appellant came to Canada) and upon return to Serbia she could live for a period in a shelter in the process of re-establishing her life in a separate residence in XXXX XXXX. In other words, the RPD notes that the evidence of past action shows that outside of the confines of the Appellant home and marriage, Mr. XXXX has not acted in a 'violent and unpredictable' manner because he did not attack his ex-wives and has never been arrested.

I would add that there is evidence of indifference to the part of Mr. XXXX towards the Appellant in that he did not assault or restrain the Appellant prior to her departure from Serbia in 2013 although as noted above, Mr. XXXX has allegedly since made threats.

The Appellant responds to this analysis by arguing that within the home, long term domestic abuse is evidence for a serious possibility that Mr. XXXX will risk arrest and sanction to somehow attack the Appellant.

In reviewing the evidence and argument, I conclude that it is the Appellant who is speculating on the behaviour of Mr. XXXX and the inadequacy of state security in her specific circumstances. I note that the Appellant reviews the evidence and is basically arguing that while the sources do identify that police intervene and abusers are arrested and found guilty, the concern of advocates is that the system is "too lenient" (Appellant's Memorandum, paragraph 42). I note the Appellant also provides references to sources which speak to the 'private problem - family matter' of the problem which would not apply to the Appellant because in this case she is now in a situation that establishes a willingness to report problems to the police and press charges.

I note the RPD has reached its conclusion through reasoned inference based on the available evidence including the profile of the agent of persecution (older, educated, with no history of criminality) and the availability of state support mechanisms (existence of shelters - RPD Record, p. 8). This also takes into consideration the perhaps less than optimal approach of the police in not severely punishing domestic abusers. The RPD reviewed the profile of Mr. XXXX to conclude that the existing state protection mechanisms would provide adequate protection in this specific case (RPD Record, p. 9).

In conclusion, I note that the burden is on the Appellant to show that her risk of persecution at the hands of Mr. XXXX is a serious possibility. In this case the RPD has reviewed the literature on state protection in XXXX XXXX and finds that it is adequate. I note that the police have had active interaction with the Appellant in the past on issues unrelated to domestic violence and have been responsive in the case of an attack on her son by a neighbour and a sexual assault on her person by an unknown assailant (RPD Record, p. 100-114). I find the analysis of the RPD with respect to the mechanisms of state protection as they apply to the specific circumstances of the Appellant persuasive and this is in a situation where the Appellant has not tested the capacity of state security instruments to act on her behalf in the past. I note that the RPD has also identified the mechanisms of support with respect to how the Appellant would re-establish herself in XXXX XXXX. I conclude that the RPD did not err in its determination and I agree with the conclusion.
For all these reasons, I confirm the determination of the RPD, namely, that Ms. XXXX XXXX is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection".

Therefore, the appeal is dismissed. Stephen J. Gallagher Stephen J. Gallagher May 24, 2016 Date /kp 1 Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution: Guidelines Issued by the Chairperson.
